chapter_title: Immersive Audio: Sound Effects and Music Integration
chapter_summary:
Sound is a powerful, often underestimated, element in game development. It can dramatically enhance player immersion, provide crucial feedback, and evoke strong emotions. Think about the satisfying "thwack" of a successful hit, the ominous background hum of a dungeon, or the joyful jingle of collecting a coin. Without these auditory cues, games can feel sterile and less responsive. In Unity, managing audio primarily revolves around `AudioClip` assets, `AudioSource` components, and `AudioListener` components. An `AudioClip` is simply your imported sound file (like a .wav or .mp3). When you import an audio file into Unity, it becomes an `AudioClip` asset, and you can configure its settings in the Inspector, such as "Load Type" (e.g., Decompress On Load for short sounds, Streaming for music) and "Compression Format" to balance quality and file size. For background music, you'll often want a high-quality, possibly streaming, clip. For quick sound effects, a compressed, decompress-on-load clip is usually sufficient.

To play an `AudioClip` in your game, you need an `AudioSource` component. An `AudioSource` acts like a speaker in your game world. You attach it to a `GameObject` (e.g., a player character for footsteps, a button for a click sound, or an empty `GameObject` for background music). Once attached, you assign an `AudioClip` to its "AudioClip" slot. For background music, you'll typically set "Play On Awake" to true and "Loop" to true so it starts playing automatically when the scene loads and repeats indefinitely. For sound effects, you often want to play them programmatically in response to an event, such as a collision or a button press. Instead of "Play On Awake", you'd call `audioSource.PlayOneShot(clip)` from a script, which is ideal for overlapping sounds without stopping the current one. A common mistake is using `audioSource.Play()` for multiple quick sound effects, which will interrupt the previous sound if it's still playing. `PlayOneShot` is designed for this scenario, allowing multiple instances of a sound to play concurrently.

The `AudioListener` component is the "ear" in your game world. Every scene must have exactly one `AudioListener` for any sound to be heard. By default, Unity attaches an `AudioListener` to your Main Camera, which is usually where you want it, as the player's perspective is typically tied to the camera. The `AudioListener` processes all `AudioSource` outputs and sends them to your actual speakers. For 3D sound, which adds realism by making sounds appear to come from specific locations in your game world, you'll adjust the "Spatial Blend" property on the `AudioSource`. A "Spatial Blend" of 0 (2D) means the sound is heard equally regardless of the `AudioSource`'s position relative to the `AudioListener`. A "Spatial Blend" of 1 (3D) means the sound will attenuate (get quieter) as the `AudioSource` moves further from the `AudioListener`, and its panning (left/right balance) will change based on its position. You can also customize the 3D sound settings, such as the "Min Distance" and "Max Distance" for attenuation, and the "Volume Rolloff" curve, to fine-tune how quickly the sound fades with distance.

Managing multiple sound effects and music tracks can quickly become complex, especially when you want to control their overall volume or apply global effects. This is where Unity's Audio Mixer comes in handy. An Audio Mixer allows you to create groups for different types of audio (e.g., "Music," "SFX," "Voice"). You then route your `AudioSource` components to these groups. Each group in the mixer can have its own volume control, Mute/Solo toggles, and even effects like reverb or equalization. This provides a centralized way to manage your game's soundscape. For example, you can easily implement a master volume slider, or separate sliders for music and sound effects, by exposing parameters from your mixer groups to your scripts. When designing your audio, consider the emotional impact you want to achieve. A sudden silence can be as impactful as a loud explosion. Use sound to guide the player, provide feedback on their actions, and build the atmosphere that defines your game.

screens.title: Immersive Audio: Sound Effects and Music Integration
screens.subtitle: Use sound to guide players, signal feedback, and build emotion

narration.text: Sound is one of the fastest ways to change how a player experiences a scene. In this lesson you will learn the practical building blocks Unity provides: audio assets become AudioClip objects, speakers in the scene are AudioSource components, and the player's ear is an AudioListener. You'll also learn simple rules for when to stream music versus load short effects into memory, how to play overlapping sound effects without cutting previous sounds, and why spatial blend makes sounds feel part of the world. We'll walk through a small, hands-on setup: a looping background music track attached to a MusicManager object and a jump or coin sound played from the player using PlayOneShot. Along the way I'll point out common mistakes — like using Play for sounds that should overlap, or accidentally having more than one AudioListener — and explain how Audio Mixer groups let you control music and SFX independently. By the end, you'll be able to import clips, configure sources for both music and effects, and make simple mixer groups to control overall volume and mood.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Audio assets, sources, and the listener together form a controllable soundscape; use PlayOneShot for overlapping effects and Audio Mixers to manage categories like Music and SFX.

narration.text: These objectives guide the practical skills you'll practice. First, you'll understand how sound effects and music shape immersion and player feedback. That means recognizing how a single coin jingle or the choice to silence music can change emotion and pacing. Second, you'll learn how to import and configure audio clips in Unity, choosing appropriate load types and compression settings so your game balances quality and performance. Third, you'll work with AudioSource components to play one-shot sound effects and looping background music, including when to use PlayOneShot versus Play. Finally on this screen you'll begin to control properties like volume, pitch, and spatial blend so sounds behave as 2D UI cues or 3D world sounds. Each of these skills is practical: you'll attach a MusicManager, add an AudioSource to the player, and route sources into mixer groups for centralized control. Together these objectives let you build a small but complete soundscape for a scene.

screens.title: Why audio matters: immersion, feedback, and emotion
screens.subtitle: Sound shapes perceived responsiveness and mood

narration.text: Sound is not decoration — it directs attention and confirms action. When a player collects a coin, a short jingle provides immediate feedback that the action succeeded. When a corridor is silent except for a low hum, that silence primes the player for tension. In practice this means you should treat sound design as a layer of interaction design: choose sounds that make actions feel satisfying and choose music that supports the intended emotion. A common mistake is to overload scenes with competing sounds; clarity comes from prioritizing feedback sounds and using mixer groups to balance them. Another misconception is that louder always equals better; loudness must be matched to context, and sudden silence can be an intentional tool. As a concrete example, use a quick, compressed AudioClip for a coin pickup so it occupies little memory and plays instantly, while a long ambient track should stream to avoid loading delays. The takeaway: plan which actions need instant feedback, which background layers set mood, and organize clips so you can tune them centrally. Think about one specific action in your game and ask: does the sound you choose make that action feel clearer or more impactful?

keyIdea.title: Takeaway
keyIdea.text: Sound should clarify actions and shape emotion; design with intent and balance using mixer groups.

screens.title: AudioClip: importing and configuration
screens.subtitle: Choose the right load and compression for each clip

narration.text: An AudioClip is the Unity representation of an imported sound file such as WAV or MP3. When you bring a clip into your Project window it becomes an AudioClip asset you can assign to AudioSource components. Two practical settings control how a clip behaves at runtime: Load Type and Compression Format. For short sound effects that must play instantly, Decompress On Load typically gives the lowest latency because the data is uncompressed into memory at load time. For long background music tracks, Streaming reduces memory use by reading data from disk as it plays. Compression balances file size and fidelity; compressed formats reduce size but can affect audio quality. The choice depends on the clip's purpose and memory budget. A common mistake is making every clip streaming — streaming many short sounds can add disk IO and latency. Another pitfall is ignoring import previews; always listen to your compressed output so you can tune quality. Example: for a coin jingle, set Decompress On Load and small compression; for a 3-minute ambient track, set Streaming and a higher-quality compression format. After import, you can assign the AudioClip to AudioSource components in the Inspector and test playback immediately in the Editor.

keyIdea.title: Tip
keyIdea.text: Use Decompress On Load for short SFX and Streaming for long music tracks to balance latency and memory.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › AudioClip Import
Definition

Import & configure AudioClip

Decide load type and compression based on clip length and performance requirements.

Load Types
  • Decompress On Load — low latency for short SFX.
  • Streaming — read from disk, good for long music.
  • Compressed In Memory — balance size and speed.
Compression
Choose compression formats to reduce file size while listening for artifacts that hurt clarity. Test compressed output before finalizing.
Common Mistake
Streaming every clip causes excessive disk access and latency for short sounds. Reserve streaming for long tracks.
Concrete example
Coin jingle: Decompress On Load for instant playback. 3-minute ambient: Streaming to save RAM.
Why this matters
Correct import settings prevent audio lag and keep builds small while preserving quality where it counts.

screens.title: AudioSource: attaching and common properties
screens.subtitle: Make a GameObject speak: play, loop, pitch, and volume

narration.text: An AudioSource is the in-scene speaker that plays an AudioClip. You attach it to a GameObject that best represents where the sound should originate: a player for footsteps, a UI button for click sounds, or an empty GameObject for music. Important properties include Play On Awake and Loop for music that should start automatically, Volume and Pitch to tune loudness and character, and Spatial Blend to control 2D versus 3D behavior. For sound effects that can overlap, call PlayOneShot from script. PlayOneShot plays a clip immediately without stopping other sounds on that source, which is ideal for repetitive pickups like coins. By contrast, Play will start playback on the source but replace any currently playing clip on that same source. Attach multiple AudioSources or use PlayOneShot to avoid unwanted interruptions. A practical setup: add an AudioSource to the Player GameObject, uncheck Play On Awake for SFX, keep Loop off, and expose the clip in the Inspector so designers can swap sounds without changing code. This pattern keeps audio flexible and reusable across different GameObjects. AudioSource: attaching and common properties means use playoneshot for event-driven sfx and configure play on awake + loop for background music sources.. In practical terms, make a gameobject speak: play, loop, pitch, and volume. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Best practice
keyIdea.text: Use PlayOneShot for event-driven SFX and configure Play On Awake + Loop for background music sources.

Play On Awake & Loop

PlayOneShot vs Play
PlayOneShot allows overlapping instances; Play replaces current playback on that source.
Volume & Pitch

Practical example
Add an AudioSource to Player, uncheck Play On Awake, expose an AudioClip field in a script, and call PlayOneShot when the player jumps to allow multiple jump sounds to overlap during rapid actions.
Common mistake
Using a single AudioSource with Play for every SFX will interrupt previously playing sounds and feel brittle.
Key Takeaway

AudioSource settings determine whether a clip behaves like an ambient layer or an instant event; choose accordingly.

screens.title: AudioListener: the game's ear
screens.subtitle: Why a single listener matters and typical placement

narration.text: The AudioListener is the receiver of all audio in a Unity scene. Think of it as the player's ear: it samples audio output from every AudioSource and sends a combined signal to the system speakers. Typically, Unity attaches an AudioListener to the Main Camera by default, which matches player perspective in most games. It's important there is only one active AudioListener; having multiple listeners can produce unexpected behavior or duplicated audio. If your game switches cameras, move the AudioListener to whichever camera represents the player's current viewpoint. For spatial audio to behave logically, ensure the listener's transform matches the player's or camera's position and orientation. A practical example: in a first-person scene keep the AudioListener on the main camera so footsteps and ambient sounds pan and attenuate correctly as the player moves. Misconceptions include thinking you need multiple listeners for multiplayer splitscreen; handle per-player audio differently or mute non-local audio rather than adding more listeners. The core insight is to centralize the game's listening point to match the player's experience. AudioListener: the game's ear means place one audiolistener on the camera representing the player's perspective; avoid multiple active listeners.. In practical terms, why a single listener matters and typical placement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reminder
keyIdea.text: Place one AudioListener on the camera representing the player's perspective; avoid multiple active listeners.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › AudioListener
Core Concept

The game's ear and correct placement

Use a single AudioListener that follows the player's viewpoint so 3D audio pans and attenuates as expected.

Typical setup
Attach the listener to the Main Camera to match player perspective.
Pitfall
Multiple active listeners can produce duplicate or confusing audio behavior.
Multiplayer note
For split-screen experiences, avoid enabling multiple listeners; route audio carefully per player instead.
Concrete example
If the player pivots, the AudioListener should move with the camera so sounds pan from left to right correctly as objects move relative to the player.

screens.title: Spatial Blend and 3D audio
screens.subtitle: Make sounds feel attached to world positions

narration.text: Spatial Blend controls whether a sound is heard equally everywhere (2D) or positioned in 3D space to attenuate and pan with distance and position. A Spatial Blend of 0 treats the source as a 2D cue — useful for UI sounds that should not change with camera position. A Spatial Blend of 1 enables 3D behavior so sounds get quieter as they move away and pan across stereo channels. To tune 3D audio further, set Min Distance and Max Distance so the sound stays full-volume within a certain radius and then fades with a selected Volume Rolloff curve. Use these controls to make footsteps, monster growls, and environmental ambiences feel anchored in the world. For example, set a close Min Distance for a near explosion so it feels loud at the player's position, and a larger Max Distance for ambient storm sounds. A common misunderstanding is to set Spatial Blend to 1 but leave distances too small, which makes sounds cut off abruptly; tune rolloff curves for natural fades. Always test with the AudioListener moving around the scene to verify the intended effect.

keyIdea.title: Practical tip
keyIdea.text: Use Spatial Blend = 0 for UI, 1 for world sounds; adjust Min/Max distance and rolloff for smooth attenuation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Spatial Blend
Process Flow

2D vs 3D audio and attenuation

Set Spatial Blend along with Min/Max distance and Volume Rolloff to make sounds fade and pan naturally in space.

Steps to tune 3D audio
  1. Set Spatial Blend to 1 for positional behavior.
  2. Choose Min Distance for full-volume radius.
  3. Set Max Distance for when the sound fades to inaudible.
  4. Pick Volume Rolloff curve for natural attenuation.
Concrete example
Monster growl: Spatial Blend = 1, Min Distance small so close ups are loud, Max Distance large so it can be heard from afar and pan across speakers.
Spatial = 0
Use for UI or global cues that should not change with position.
Spatial = 1
Use for world sounds that need direction and distance behavior.
Check
Move the camera around the source to verify panning and attenuation feel natural.

screens.title: Audio Mixer: grouping, routing, and central control
screens.subtitle: Manage Music, SFX, and Voice with mixer groups

narration.text: As your project grows, controlling dozens of AudioSources directly becomes unwieldy. An Audio Mixer provides a centralized interface to create groups, route AudioSources into those groups, and adjust levels or effects for whole categories at once. Typical groups are Music, SFX, and Voice. Route each AudioSource's Output to the appropriate mixer group so you can mute or lower a category with one control. Mixers also let you add effects such as reverb or equalization on a channel-wide basis, and expose parameters so UI sliders or scripts can change group volume at runtime. For example, expose the SFX group's volume to a settings slider and let players lower only SFX while keeping music playing. A misconception is that you must use a mixer for every project; small prototypes can get by without one, but mixers pay off quickly when balancing multiple layers of audio. The practical goal here is to route AudioSources into the Mixer, create sensible groups, and expose key parameters for runtime control. Audio Mixer: grouping, routing, and central control means mixers centralize volume control and effects, making balancing and runtime adjustments simpler.. In practical terms, manage music, sfx, and voice with mixer groups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Why use a Mixer
keyIdea.text: Mixers centralize volume control and effects, making balancing and runtime adjustments simpler.

Create groups and route audio for central control

Use the Audio Mixer to group sources and expose parameters for UI and scripts.

Common groups
  • Music
  • SFX
  • Voice
Routing
Set an AudioSource's Output to the chosen mixer group so effects and volume affect that source.

Misconception
A mixer is not required early, but it saves time when you must tune levels across many sources.

screens.title: PlayOneShot: reliable SFX playback
screens.subtitle: Why PlayOneShot is ideal for overlapping sound effects

narration.text: PlayOneShot is the preferred method for event-driven sound effects that may overlap, such as coin collections or rapid jumps. It plays the specified clip immediately without stopping any clip currently playing on the same AudioSource. By contrast, calling Play on a source will begin playback but interrupt any existing sound on that source. This distinction matters when many identical events can occur in quick succession. To use PlayOneShot, expose an AudioClip and an AudioSource on a Player GameObject, then call PlayOneShot from your sound helper script when the event occurs. The chapter supplies a canonical pattern: create a SoundEffectPlayer component that caches the player's AudioSource, holds a public AudioClip reference, and calls playerAudioSource. PlayOneShot(jumpSoundClip) inside a PlayJumpSound method. Attach this component to the Player and call PlayJumpSound from your PlayerController's Jump method. This pattern keeps audio logic separate from movement logic and prevents audio interruptions during rapid actions. Test by triggering the event repeatedly and listen for overlapping instances playing cleanly. PlayOneShot: reliable SFX playback means separate sfx playback into a small component that calls playoneshot to allow overlapping audio while keeping movement code focused.. In practical terms, why playoneshot is ideal for overlapping sound effects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Code insight
keyIdea.text: Separate SFX playback into a small component that calls PlayOneShot to allow overlapping audio while keeping movement code focused.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › PlayOneShot
Code Walkthrough

SoundEffectPlayer pattern

A small component caches the AudioSource, exposes an AudioClip, and plays it via PlayOneShot when requested by gameplay code.

// SoundEffectPlayer.cs (attached to Player)
using UnityEngine;

public class SoundEffectPlayer : MonoBehaviour
{
  public AudioClip jumpSoundClip;
  private AudioSource playerAudioSource; // Assign this in Inspector

  void Awake()
  {
    playerAudioSource = GetComponent();
    if (playerAudioSource == null)
    {
      Debug.LogError("AudioSource component not found on Player!");
    }
  }

  public void PlayJumpSound()
  {
    if (playerAudioSource != null && jumpSoundClip != null)
    {
      playerAudioSource.PlayOneShot(jumpSoundClip);
    }
  }
}
Runtime check
Call PlayJumpSound from your PlayerController when the jump occurs and verify multiple quick jumps still play sounds without interruption.
Why this pattern
  • Keeps audio separate from movement logic.
  • Prevents audio clipping by allowing overlapped instances.
  • Makes it easy to swap clips in the Inspector without changing code.
Key Takeaway

PlayOneShot is the right tool for short, repeatable SFX that must not cut previous sounds.

screens.title: Hands-on: Add looping background music
screens.subtitle: Create a MusicManager and set its AudioSource

narration.text: Let's walk through a short hands-on setup for background music. First, create an empty GameObject in your scene and name it MusicManager. Add an AudioSource component to that object and assign your imported music AudioClip to the AudioClip slot. For continuous playback set Play On Awake and Loop to true so the track starts automatically when the scene loads and repeats. Adjust the Volume to a comfortable level relative to SFX. If you use an Audio Mixer, route this AudioSource's Output to the Music mixer group so players can later adjust music level independently. A common issue is placing multiple MusicManager objects across scenes; ensure you only have one active manager at a time or implement a singleton to avoid duplicate music. Test in the Editor by pressing Play and listening for smooth loop transitions and correct volume. This small change immediately improves atmosphere and demonstrates how simple settings produce large perceptual effects. screens.title: Hands-on: Player SFX with SoundEffectPlayer
screens.subtitle: Expose clips and call PlayOneShot from gameplay code

narration.text: We'll build a Player SFX pattern that separates audio logic from movement. Attach an AudioSource component to your Player GameObject and uncheck Play On Awake and Loop. Create a SoundEffectPlayer script that stores a public AudioClip reference for the jump sound and caches the player AudioSource in Awake. Expose the AudioClip in the Inspector so designers can swap sounds without touching code. In your movement script, reference the SoundEffectPlayer and call its PlayJumpSound method when the player jumps. This method calls PlayOneShot on the cached AudioSource, ensuring the jump sound plays immediately and can overlap with other sounds. A common mistake is forgetting to assign the AudioSource on the Player — the script logs an error in Awake to help catch this. Test repeatedly: press the jump input quickly to verify overlapping instances sound correct. This approach makes SFX behaviors modular, testable, and easy to balance through the Audio Mixer if you route the player source to an SFX group. Hands-on: Player SFX with SoundEffectPlayer means a modular soundeffectplayer lets gameplay trigger sounds reliably while leaving clip selection and volume to designers and mixers.. In practical terms, expose clips and call playoneshot from gameplay code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: A modular SoundEffectPlayer lets gameplay trigger sounds reliably while leaving clip selection and volume to designers and mixers.

screens.title: Play() vs PlayOneShot()
screens.subtitle: When to use each method and what to avoid

narration.text: Understanding the difference between Play and PlayOneShot is essential for correct SFX behavior. Play starts playback of the AudioSource's assigned clip and will interrupt any clip already playing on that same source. This makes Play suitable for exclusive streams like a door creak where only one instance should exist. PlayOneShot, however, mixes the specified clip into the source's output without stopping existing audio from that source. That makes PlayOneShot ideal for repetitive, overlapping events like coin collections or gunfire bursts. A frequent beginner error is using Play for coin sounds, which results in earlier coins being cut off when multiple are picked up quickly. Another mistake is relying on many separate AudioSources for every small sound when PlayOneShot could handle overlap on a single source. Choose Play when single-instance control and direct clip replacement are required; choose PlayOneShot for short, event-driven SFX that may overlap. To check your implementation, trigger the event rapidly and observe whether multiple instances play simultaneously as intended. keyIdea.text: Use PlayOneShot for short overlapping SFX; use Play for exclusive, single-instance playback.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Play() vs PlayOneShot()
Comparison

Choose the right playback method

Play()
Starts the assigned clip on the AudioSource and will interrupt any current playback on that source. Use for exclusive sounds where you do not want overlap.
When to use
  • Long or exclusive clips like single ambient streams or unique actions.
PlayOneShot()
Plays a clip immediately without stopping sounds already playing on the same source, allowing overlap. Ideal for SFX like coins, jumps, and repeated impacts.
When to use
  • Short, repeatable SFX that should not cut each other off.
Misconception
Using many Play calls across identical sources to simulate overlap is inefficient; PlayOneShot is a cleaner solution.

screens.title: Balancing quality, memory, and runtime performance
screens.subtitle: Choose import settings and mixer strategies that scale

narration.text: Audio choices affect both player experience and build performance. Short SFX benefit from Decompress On Load because they play with low latency and usually consume small amounts of memory. Long music tracks should stream to avoid using excessive R A M. Compression reduces file size but introduces artifacts; always preview compressed audio to ensure artifacts do not harm clarity for critical cues. When many sounds play simultaneously, consider limiting simultaneous SFX or using pooled AudioSources to avoid an explosion of active sources. Use Audio Mixer groups to mute or duck categories in heavy scenes to preserve clarity. A practical rule is to profile memory and C P U with representative scenes and adjust import and compression settings until you reach acceptable performance without audible quality loss. Also consider exposing mixer volumes to let players adjust music vs SFX, which reduces perceived problems caused by player hardware differences. The final step is rigorous playtesting: listen for masking, clipping, or audible artifacts when many sounds play at once and adjust rolloff and levels accordingly. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to keep in mind: first, an AudioClip is the imported asset representing sound; choose load type and compression based on whether a clip must be low latency or memory friendly. Second, an AudioSource attached to a GameObject plays clips; use PlayOneShot for overlapping short SFX and use Play with Loop and Play On Awake for background music. Third, the AudioListener is the single 'ear' of the scene, usually attached to the Main Camera. Fourth, Spatial Blend determines 2D versus 3D behavior, controlling attenuation and panning through Min/Max distance and rolloff. Fifth, the Audio Mixer lets you group sources into Music, SFX, and Voice for centralized volume and effects, and you can expose parameters to UI and scripts. Remember these building blocks as you design, test, and iterate: import, attach, tune spatial properties, and centralize control with mixers.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Practical reminders
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to lock in core practices

narration.text: To close, keep three practical reminders front of mind. First, plan import settings: use Decompress On Load for short, low-latency effects and Streaming for long music tracks. Second, prefer PlayOneShot for event-driven SFX that must overlap and reserve Play for single-instance streams. Third, route sources into an Audio Mixer and expose group volumes so you can balance Music and SFX without changing every AudioSource. Follow these rules during development and iterate with playtesting: import and routing choices are reversible, but they shape how responsive and clear your audio feels in play. As you test, focus on whether actions feel satisfying and whether important cues remain audible when many sounds are active.
